utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletelic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naletelic? How are you feeling today?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry, mike, please. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Not great, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we were sorry that you were not with us last week. We all hope you a speedy recovery. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. With your leave, there are two matters which I'd like to raise with the Honourable Court. The first is the illness of my client. I'd like the Chamber to order the Registry to remove from the list of expert witnesses of cardiological and pulmonary diseases to appoint --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] to appoint a cardiologist and pulmonary expert who would examine my client, write down his opinion and submit it to the Chamber, because at the last examination, Your Honours, I managed to visit my client on Friday, and all the coronary diseases have been confirmed, or, rather, a major occlusion of blood vessels was established, and with the angina pectoris and the pulmonary emphysema [as interpreted] -- could produce fatal consequences. As I have already said, my client does not feel very well today either, but he is somehow managing because he does not wish to disrupt the schedule. Such an independent opinion by an independent expert witness, whether my client is up to following the hearing and participating actively in it without imperilling his health, which is at present very -- in a very grave state. Such an opinion by such an expert witness, the Chamber would take notice of the opinion of such expert witness. The second matter I wish to raise with Your Honours, I'd like to go into private session if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, as for your first request, I think this Trial Chamber is waiting for the report from the doctor who did the surgery of your client last week, and we will take your request into consideration when we read those reports. Then we will make a decision whether it is necessary for us to have an order to have an independent expert to have your client examined. Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr.Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting and we're private session -- no, we're not in private session. We may or may not need to. I'm is a little surprised given the time we were given a few days ago to hear counsel say we could be finished three witnesses in four days, which makes me wonder if the order or names of the witnesses has changed. Perhaps he could advise who these three witnesses are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Would you be kind enough to reaffirm what the witnesses are this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They will all be testifying in open session following the order as I have submitted. What I -- [In English] Everything is expected of -- [Interpretation] It all depends on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry, given the changes that have already occurred, I would still like to have the three names confirmed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are no changes at all. The only change that happened was due to the witness's sickness. Otherwise, there are absolutely no changes. The witnesses are here, Mr. Kovac, Mr. Galsnovic, Mr. Bender, right according to the sequence we submitted two weeks ago that we planned to do this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Two short remarks before we start to try to make our work easier and use your time better. We speak the same language, and I will therefore ask you to wait for the end of my question. And you have a monitor in front of you. Can you see it? Do you see it? This black dot that moves, when it stops, that will mean that the transcript is finished and that you can start your answer, especially bearing in mind that we have interpretation into two languages, English and French.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation and understanding, and let us start. Witness, first we need you to introduce yourself to the Court. So will you please briefly tell us what was your curriculum vitae up to 1990, and then briefly tell us all the positions that you held between 1990 and today.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I am Milan Kovac, I was born in 1953 in Posusje, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I completed my primary and secondary education there. In 1972, I enrolled in the faculty of economics in Zagreb. I graduated in 1978. After that, I found a job and I worked for a trading company until 1990. In 1989, I took part in the establishment of the Croat Democratic Union, because until then I was not a member of the Communist Party of Croatia. And at the founding convention on the 17th of June, 1989, I was elected to the Executive Board of the Croat Democratic Union and its chief treasurer, and thereby I became a member of the Presidency of the Croat Democratic Union. In the elections of 1990, the first democratic elections in Croatia, I was elected to the Croat state diet. In the diet, I was elected the chairman of the board for administrative affairs, and I headed that board until the end of 1992, when I was once again in the second elections. I was elected to the Croatian state diet. At that time, until 1995, I was a member of the foreign affairs board. In 1995, in the third elections, once again on the list of the Croat Democratic Union, I was elected to the Croatian state diet. I was a member of the board for human rights and national minorities and the board for emigration -- or immigration. Excuse me. In 1997, I became a Minister in the government of the Republic of Croatia, responsible for privatisation until 1999, when this ministry was abolished, and I became a Minister in the Republic of Croatia, responsible for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Until the 3rd of January 2001, the fourth parliamentary elections, when on the list for the Croat democratic union for emigration, I headed the list and was for the fourth time elected to the Croatian state diet with over 90 per cent of votes. Then when I was in the diet I was elected to chair the board for immigration, and that is the position which I still hold in the Croatian diet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, since you are one of the founders of the HDZ, can you tell the Court, what was the programme of the party? What were its principal determinants and where it was founded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Once we realised that the Communist Party systems in Eastern Europe were caving in both political and economically, after in the lands of the former Yugoslavia, things happened which for us in Croatia necessitated a commitment and organisation of the first democratic elections. The Executive Board headed by the late President Tudjman decided to form a party after -- for several months in Croatia, before we were founded, four or five political parties have already been -- were already -- had already been established with a clear programme. We were witness to -- during those days and weeks in the lands of the former Yugoslavia, we were witness how the Greater Serbian policy headed by Milosevic settled scores with democratic authorities in a non-democratic manner in KOS where they had removed their lawful leadership, then in another province, in Vojvodina, then in Montenegro. And a campaign against Croatia and Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina was under preparation. The then-Croatian political leadership in Zagreb did not react, and it was called "Croat silence." And one needed to speak out clearly and warn people of the dangers and perils looming ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you said the political leadership then, whom did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: It was the Communist Party of Croatia, the leadership of the Communist Party of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, of course try to be as concise as possible. The Honourable Court cannot follow all these events like you and I can. So please explain the ideas that you speak about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I understand. The founding of the Croatian Democratic Union, the basis, there were three basis; namely that the former Yugoslavia had to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. undergo democratisation, that a multi-party system had been introduced as well as multi-party elections, with the publication would acquire greater authority. The authority was to be decentralised and where we should have embarked upon a co-federal setup, state setup in the former Yugoslavia. Secondly, the Republic of Croatia, as well as all the other republics which comprised the former Yugoslavia, would have to secede to embrace a multi-party system, a market economy, because we were witnesses of a collapse, economic collapse throughout Yugoslavia in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. And then the creation of closer ties between the Croats living in Croatia and millions of Croats living throughout the world, which due to political and economic reasons, were fleeing from Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and other areas to other countries in order to be able to live a normal life. These were the basic concepts of the Croatian Democratic Union and with which it required a plebiscitary support of the entire Croatian nation. And fourth, speedy secession of the other former Yugoslav republication likes to the European integrations and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And in which areas was it established in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union was set up in all areas where Croats lived in that common state, primarily in the republic of Croatia. It was registered with the court in Zagreb. It was founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina and registered with the court of Sarajevo. It was founded in Australia and the United States, wherever there were big colonies of the Croatian nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the Croatian Democratic Union and its views concerning the relations with the other former republics of Yugoslavia? And a sub-question, an auxiliary one, if I may, whether in that programme of it, did it have a plan for an independent state, democratic State of Croatia and its attitude towards also the other nations of the former Yugoslavia in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union, in its programme, clearly expressed its position concerning the relationship between the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis the other former republics that there would be the respect of the 1974 Constitution which enabled all the republics self-determination up to complete and full secession. We considered the basic principle was the inviolability of the republican borders, and on that basis the Republic of Croatia demanded its recognition, which it also received from the international community on the 15th of January, 1992. And so it means the same rights to all the republics on the -- based on the principle of the Avnoj borders which were determined after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you're speaking of the Avnoj border, the internal borders dividing internally the Yugoslav territory, the republican borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As you have already answered that the Croat Democratic Union had a plebiscitary support and it had a majority in the diet in the Republic of Croatia. I apologise, Mr. Kovac, two of my questions entered the transcript without your answers. The first question was whether this was the division of territories and determination of republican borders within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And question now, the second question which we began, so the HDZ had a majority in the Croatian diet of the Republic of Croatia. Does that mean that HDZ also was implementing its policy through the diet? We could speak of the first elections, 1992, and the second elections 1992, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. Did the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does it mean -- does it mean that only the HDZ was implementing the policy through the diet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I also don't understand your question. It's a difficult one. Try to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will simplify it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How a decision passed, decisions of national interest in the national diet? Was it based on the will of the HDZ or did also other parties participate in these decision-makings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: All the major decisions of national importance for the state, for the nation, and for the citizens of Croatia were passed on the basis of consensus of all the parliamentary parties. I wonder whether Your Honours do have the data and information that in 1991, despite the absolute two-third majority the HDZ had in the national diet, a government of national unity was formed which included and encompassed all parliamentary party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My next question would be, and that is why I raised this previous question, whether the HDZ had in its programme also as a goal annexation of any part of any republic of the former Yugoslavia. And here, this would be the question: Any part of any republic of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No. No, never. All programmes of HDZ and declarations which were passed at the highest fora of the party are accessible, are public. They were and are public, and it can be seen. But the position of the HDZ was concerning this issue. Never did any official of the HDZ in the party or in the government did ever express such a position. We adhered to legality. We respected the republican borders, the inviolability of the borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You were -- you did cooperate with the late President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: At the beginning when we were founding the HDZ, we were in a practically everyday contact. Later when he became president of the republic, we did contact on the basis of the functions we had, to the extent that we needed. I think, believe I was close to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you and did he personally express views concerning annexation of other areas? I mean in a private suggestion outside the official policy framework.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No, truly never. He was only persistent, and he demanded that the Croatian people living in other republics, in Bosnia and Herzegovina as the constituent and sovereign nation together with Serbs and Bosniaks, that they have the same rights within the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then for the Croatian nation living in Serbia, in Vojvodina, that they have the rights of a national minority, as was the case in Kosovo. In Janjevo, there was an enclave, a Croatian enclave, which due to the events, past events, they had to be transferred because there was a danger, a possible threat of genocide against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you explain to Their Honours how the Croatian diet functions? What does the parliament consist of and how does it function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: In 1990, we -- it was -- we had three Chambers. And this was a relic from the communist system. It was the Chamber of Associated Labour. I don't know how that can be translated. Then of municipalities, and the socio-political Chamber. With the passing of the new constitution in 1990, that model was replaced with the Chamber of Representatives in the diet, and in 1993, with the regionalisation of Croatia into counties, we had an additional Chamber which was then introduced, the Chamber of Counties. So we had two Chambers. And from the year 2000 onwards, the new authorities have suppressed that one, the second Chamber of the Counties, and we only have the house -- the Chamber of Representatives today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember in which month of 1993 the senate or the Chamber of Counties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I think it was in May 1993. It was in spring. It was then that also elections were held for the senate, for the Chamber of Counties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First question: Were you a representative at the constituent assembly of the diet when the constitution was passed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware of the contents of the articles of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: As far as a deputy has to be acquainted with the constitution, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think I am quite well acquainted with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does the constitution prescribe what are the decisions which have to be taken by both and approved by both Chambers of the diet?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: One of the fundamental questions was -- which had to be approved by both Chambers was the regional setup, the regional organisation of the Republic of Croatia, the ratification of international agreements, association, disassociation of the republic. Then if the army is to be sent to other countries, that was within the competent of the parliament, and approval had to be gained from both chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you mentioned the sending of the army to another country, that is in case of declaration of war, in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: However, we will come to that issue a bit later. We would be interested if you could explain to this Chamber primarily whether the Republic of Croatia had a particular relationship, a special relationship with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia did have a particular special attitude towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. It also stems from the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, where it states that the Republic of Croatia must care for its compatriots wherever they live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you explain? Why did the -- in the constituent assembly -- in the constitution did the parliament adopt this article, and could you say something about the diaspora, the Croatian diaspora and how many people went abroad?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: According to the latest assessment it's hard to determine the exact number, but some authoritative institutions have submitted information that Croats living outside the borders of Croatia amount to 3 to 4 million. And that is approximately as much -- as many as today live in the Republic of Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. I -- you can continue. I just wanted to explain to this Chamber the reasons of this provision.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: With this, I did not mean that the Croatia people living in Bosnia and Herzegovina represented a part of the diaspora. That is a nation living there for the past thousands of years in that area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a nation according to all constitutions and provisions has the same right or should have the same right as the other two nations living in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are constituent nations, that they enjoy equal rights, are on equal footing and sovereignty which is described in the latest agreement which was resolving the problems of Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely the Dayton Accord. The Republic of Croatia and the leadership of Croatia always endeavoured that the Croatian nation attains these rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina, always considering and taking as a starting point that Bosnia and Herzegovina must be an independent, free, unified country with an internal organisational setup which would correspond to the needs of all three nations. In view of the fact also that politically the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, they have a close transportation links, overlapping transportation links. There's the entire network of infrastructure. It's normal for the Republic of Croatia to see, and it's in her interest to have a stable Bosnia and Herzegovina, because if Bosnia and Herzegovina are unstable, Croatia cannot be stable either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, as a deputy in the diet of the Republic of Croatia, did you attend all the important sessions of the diet? I'm stressing important sessions because I know you couldn't have attended all of them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I am one of the deputies who had the fewest -- who was absent the fewest times from the sessions in the diet. And this refers to the entire period of the past 12 years. I attended all of the most important sessions where important and decisive decisions, upon for the fate of the country, were passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the diet ever pass a decision that Croatia was at war with Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No, it never passed such a decision. Only in the diet a discussion was held concerning the crisis which existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the aggression of the Yugoslav army and the occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by that army and the Serbian forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And later, a discussion was held because of the conflict which erupted between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and how to stop it. Because also of the great number of Croatian refugees in the Republic of Croatia, we already had to take in a million refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina also. It means that every fourth inhabitant of Croatia was either a refugee or -- so we insisted that these conflicts be stopped as soon as possible in Bosnia and Herzegovina in view of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the diet ever get or take notice of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina has proclaimed for on the Republic of Croatia [As interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I am not aware of such -- Bosnia and Herzegovina's decision. At that time, I was a member of the foreign affairs board of the diet. We never received an official note or warning by Bosnia-Herzegovina that allegedly Croatia has committed aggression or was trying to occupy parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Precisely. That was to be my next question. So did Bosnia and Herzegovina in any way whatsoever declare to the Republic of Croatia that it considered itself at war with Croatia and that it held that Croatia had undertaken a partial occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Croatia occupy parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No, it never. It never committed any aggression towards Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were diplomatic relations maintained between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993 onward?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: After the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 1st of March, 1992, when the Croat people voted for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Let's talk about these diplomatic relations if you would be so kind. When were they established and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia was one of the first countries to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was the first or one of the first?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I believe it was the first and the first to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have some problems with the channels. Is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French booth is asking that the second witness's microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, will you please be so kind as to tell us? We were saying that the Republic of Croatia was the first one to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: And the first one to send its ambassador to Sarajevo. It established its consular offices in Tuzla, Bihac, and Mostar, and was in permanent communication with the Bosnia and Herzegovinian authorities through various state organisations, through embassies and consular offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which are these authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina elected to the parliament in Sarajevo its representatives, and they took part in the exercise of power in Sarajevo. They elected their member to the Presidency, participated in the deliberations of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the authorities in the Republic of Croatia communicated with the official representatives of the Bosnian and Croat people in Sarajevo, because we know that in late 1991, the representatives of the Serb people in the parliament quit the parliament and founded the parliament of Republika Srpska after the referendum conducted in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how was it in 1993? Which are the official authorities in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina, say, from the middle and through the latter half? Who did you communicate with in your -- during your official visits or talks or just communication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: At that time, I was not part of the executive, and I -- but I do know that the government of the Republic of Croatia, through its activities endeavoured to establish contact both with representatives of the Croat and the Bosniak peoples in Sarajevo. However, after the conflict in 1993 with the Muslim army and the Croat defence council, as far as I can remember, the Croat representatives in the Sarajevo authorities refused to continue in that joint government, and it gave rise to problems in the communication between Zagreb and Sarajevo. I remember how Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who said about himself that he was the president of the Presidency, even if a Rump Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina [As interpreted], was often received by Mr. Tudjman in Zagreb, and they talked there about the solution of these problems which have occurred because the cooperation was blocked and because the Croat people had decided not to participate under such -- in government institutions under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you personally know or were you present when Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was accepted, was received as the head of state or representative of a people? How was he treated when he came on state visits or, rather, during talks with President Tudjman that his government or any other diplomatic communication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: He was received as the representative of the Muslim people, as a member of the Party of Democratic Action. The biggest Muslim organisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because he -- that is what he was, a representative of the Muslim people. As the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we know why, founded the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, later on Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, because of the policy pursued at the time by the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We shall come to those things that you personally know because you had personally had a hand in it later on, but now I'd like to round off the subject of the Croatian diet. And my last question concerning diplomatic relations in 1992, 1993. That is the time that you talked about. Were the diplomatic relations ever broken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Officially, no, never. But they were fraught with difficulties, and the communication with Sarajevo was difficult right up to this conclusion of the Washington Agreement when -- in 1994 when the joint institutions of the Bosniak and Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Chamber who drew up, who was the author of the Croatian policy? Was it the president? Was it the diet, or was it the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the policy was drawn up in accordance with the constitution of Croatia which laid down the terms of reference of different branches of power. The executive, legislative, and judiciary. In that system, the -- President Tudjman had certain powers. The parliament had its powers. The government also had its powers. All the key issues and problems and decisions were taken by the diet of the Republic of Croatia. Naturally, both the president and the government had exercised their powers specified by the constitution and statute which authorised them to take individual decisions. The HDZ, as the largest party in the parliament throughout those ten years, adopted its guidelines, its platforms, its declarations. It was done by the party bodies, and the convention -- and the party conventions which adopted decisions and decided on the manner of the functioning of the state in all aspects. And then naturally the executive and the legislative power, where the HDZ had the majority, it then drafted the projected -- the policy for the years to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And Mr. Kovac, I think this will be my last question before the break. Could President Tudjman can independent decisions about, for instance, sending Croatian troops to some other independent state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No. No, he could not do it. The constitution would not allow it, and he did not do that. Only the Croatian diet can decide to send the troops to any other foreign state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will tell you that it is alleged here not only that President Tudjman had ordered that but that he also occupied parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina with a view to annexing those parts of the territory to the Republic of Croatia. What will you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: If it is claimed here, I don't think it is claimed in good faith, nor is it true. President Tudjman never sent any troops to any other state. Had he done that, the Croatian diet would have known it and stopped such decision from being operationalised. But in his programme as an historian, as an outstanding politician privately or publicly did President Tudjman ever talk about the annexation or occupation of parts of other states, because to my mind it would be crazy to say when your country is occupied, when one-third of your country is under occupation and the one who has occupied wants it to change republican borders and annex that part of the Republic of Croatia to Serbia, to then advocate the petitioning or the occupation of a neighbouring state where -- and the sacred principle governing President Tudjman was the one on the basis of which Croatia was recognised by the international community. That was the inviolability of the republican borders in the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my last question before the break. Gentlemen from the Prosecution claim that the Croatian had its state agents in Bosnia-Herzegovina who carried that out. What will you say to that? Agents, that is coordinators.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I have to say that this is the first time I hear anything like that. The Republic of Croatia had its embassy, its consulate, in the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, through which it pursued its policy and cooperated with Bosnia-Herzegovina as with all the other states. And I must say I am pretty taken aback by the statement that there are some agents or coordinators who would be working apart from the system of government. That did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is now time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I want to apologise for being late. I was reading something and was in another world. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm so impressed by the way you treat us. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'd like to round off the subject, so my last question will be: Did the Croatian national diet, that is both chambers of the diet, ever take a decision to send military formations of the Republic of Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina so that they would participate on the Croat side, on the side of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the conflict or war against Muslims and their armed component, that is the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No, never. Our parliament never discussed it, and it never took a decision to send the troops to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my final question: Can anyone do it without the diet?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: No. Nobody can do it because the constitution lays down the duties of the diet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And had some unit of the Croatian army illegally entered Bosnia and Herzegovina, would that be sanctioned in the Republic of Croatia as undermining the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it would have been done, and we did that at the time of the aggression of the Yugoslav people's army and Montenegro and Serbia against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, that response doesn't make sense. He's saying they did undermine the constitution, so it doesn't make sense. So I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think it needs clarification

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have to take care of the transcript, Witness, and indeed your answer was interpreted somewhat vaguely. Let us clear it up. Would the legislature of the Republic of Croatia sanction, I mean courts, the prosecutor's office, investigating bodies, would they sanction unlawful conduct, for instance if a unit of the Croatian army arbitrarily, on its own, went to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is what the transcript says, and I want us to clarify. What did you mean when you said that Croatia sanctioned -- adopted sanctions against, punished, in the case of aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army, Montenegro and Serbia against the Republic of Croatia? What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I understood that you asked me what -- if and what Republic of Croatia would do if foreign troops entered the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Well, then, so what did it do? What did the Republic of Croatia do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Croatian national diet proclaim the aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army, Montenegro and Serbia against Republic of Croatia and notified all the international institutions, the United Nations, international associations, and all the other states of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Now I understand. I hope we've clarified the transcript. Both questions I asked had to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that matter I think we've cleared up, so we can move on. What do you personally know about the referendum conducted in Bosnia-Herzegovina in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I know about the referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina because as a member in -- of the Croatian national diet, I was elected with another ten MPs to be one of the international parliamentarians monitoring the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 29th of February and the 1st of March, I was present in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina together with Italian, Spanish, German, and other parliamentarians, and we supervised the conduct of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know the outcome? Do you know the results?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, I was designated to be together with Italian and Belgian, I believe, parliamentarians in Central Bosnia, in the municipality of Prozor, in several places where the referendum was conducted, and we were to submit a report to the leader of the parliamentarian mission in Sarajevo after the referendum. The referendum was in order in those places where we were because the Croats constituted a majority in those places where we were present. And when we returned to Sarajevo, we reported about our work and our observations, and the final result of the referendum is common knowledge. The Croat people en masse responded, and 96 per cent of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Croat ethnicity voted in the affirmative. About 68 per cent of the Bosniaks likewise. And as far as I know, the Serbs did not take part in the referendum. In late 1991, they had their own referendum on the establishment of Republika Srpska and its joining the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean by "participation?" Do you mean they voted for independence or they didn't come out of the house? I didn't quite understand well the percentages. And you say you participate, not participate. Does that mean that somebody did not come out of his house to vote or that they voted in some other way? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the question of Her Honour. What do you answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I meant that the Croat people came out and supported the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is they voted for. Ninety-six per cent voted for. The Muslim people voted. Sixty-eight per cent voted for and the Serb people did not participate in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, as an observer or through the HDZ, did you know what was the referendum question and whether the HDZ had different question, the so-called "Livno question," which is here shown in a different light? Do you know anything about that, the so-called "Livno question"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know the details because I was not in Livno. So I have no way of knowing. But I learned from the media that the Croat representatives and the leadership of the Croat people in Livno requested that the question already defined the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some thought that they wanted a unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina as before. Others wanted to have the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina regulated, needless to say, within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. If I understand you correctly, you mean that the representatives of the Croat people in Bosnia wanted not only to vote for the independence but also to have a question which would encompass the future internal organisation of Bosnia and of Herzegovina, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we understand the witness told us he was not there. All the information he told us was from the media. So we cannot get anywhere. So drop this question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right you are, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We will focus on Croatia in 1993, and my first question will be whether in the state diet there was a discussion on Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely -- in other words, when did the conflicts begin among Muslims and Croats, and whether you are aware how many agreements had been signed by the Muslim element in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian state and how many peace accords?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: After the outbreaks of conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina between the Croats and the Bosniaks, the Croatian diet did discuss -- did devote some time to this subject and discuss it. And after the report submitted to the parliament, submitted by the government, the Croatian diet then also adopted, passed resolution. I believe it was in April 1993 and -- where it chose members. It appointed a delegation imposed of all members of parties present in the parliament and then assigned them to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We described this as mission -- a goodwill mission. They were to go to find out what the situation was, what were the causes of the conflict, to speak to both parties on both sides. And they were trusted to try to find a way of overcoming the conflict and finding a resolution, a peaceful resolution to this conflict. After that visit, we in the diet received the report of that delegation, their, also, findings --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have ID305, which hasn't been translated. And I will not discuss it; however, the witness can describe it. And once it is translated, I will submit it as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my first question will be: This document that you're seeing now, was this the parliamentary mission? Who was a member of the mission, where did they go, what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no objection to using this document, but at least if we can get a copy of the Bosnian version or the version in Serbo-Croatian, because we don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You are obliged to furnish in document no matter in what kind of language, to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already submitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Is there any indication --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the report of the parliamentary Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mission of the state diet which visited Mostar at the beginning of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: My apologies. I have this here. It's numbered 304.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said 305. That's why I was confused.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is 305. It was inadvertently marked by the Defence as 326, and a direction was made before court began today. So.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have a copy. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you inform this Chamber? Maybe you could also read out parts of the document. The interpreters will be able to help us. Maybe you could inform the -- this Chamber on this document, the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that the Croatian parliament took a unanimous decision to send a mission to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to visit Kiseljak, Busovaca, Travnik. They would then talk with the representatives of the Croatian people as well as of the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then to report back to the Croatian diet, to the Croatian parliament what they have found out, what are the causes of the conflict, and how to resolve the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did they visit Mostar? On which date did the delegation arrive and when did it leave Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The delegation visited Medjugorje on the 30th of April. It had a meeting with the authorities of the HVO, then with medical military staff and their representatives. Then on the 1st of May, they had a meeting with the representatives -- with the representatives of the authorities of Tuzla and north-eastern Bosnia. On the same day, they had a meeting at 10.00 with the president of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina Milo Akmadzic and Milo Boras, who was a member of the BH Presidency. Then at 1.00 p.m., a meeting with the regional representatives of the regional board of HDZ for Herzegovina. However, on the next day, they were to go and move into Bosnia, to travel to Bosnia. The international forces informed them that they could not ensure their safe passage so that that visit -- that part of visit was -- did not take place to those cities and towns in central and northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who were the members of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The delegation consisted of Drago Krpina from HDZ, who was also the leader of that mission. Mato Arlovic from the Social Democratic Party, SDP, who is also today still a deputy, as well as Mr. Krpina. Mato Arlovic is today the vice-president of the Croatian parliament, and he is originally from the Social Democratic Party. Then Ivica Vrkic, the Croatian People's Party, HNS; Mr. Mirko Madjor from the Croatian Farmers Party, HSS; then the deputy president of HSLS, Mr. Velimir Terzic. He was the deputy of the head of the mission. Unfortunately, he is deceased now. And Vera Stanic from HDZ. She also passed away last year. And Mr. Branimir Pasecky from HDZ also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The question. I'm asking you whether Mr. Secks and Mr. Sanader, in April or May of 1993, were they present in any delegation which would visit Herzegovina or Mostar or these places, or Medjugorje in the negotiations with the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: After this visit, which yielded no results and the conflict continued, the clashes continued, we attempted once again to send a party delegation to talk with the SDA representatives, and I believe that was in Medjugorje, where the meeting in fact was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: It was either May or June. It was the spring of 1993. And except for these two persons, I don't know who else were members of that mission, but I do know that the meeting took place. I believe at the time also in Medjugorje, a meeting was held with the international representatives, Mr. Stoltenberg, and that also President Tudjman, at the invitation of the international community, was present, as well as Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Also at the invitation of the international community, where an attempt was made to try to find the ways and means of stopping the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have heard a witness testify. You've described this parliamentary delegations which went there, the first one, the second one in Medjugorje. We have heard that they -- that they have come to order HDZ and HVO and SDA to order what they are to do, particularly, Mr. Seks and Mr. Senada were mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I don't think that's possible that as deputies in the national diet that they go and issue orders in Bosnia-Herzegovina to tell Croatian people there what to do. I wasn't present, however, but I do know they asked that at any price the conflict be stopped because at the time, Croatia, as I have mentioned before, was facing economic collapse. It was blocked in all areas where every day thousands upon thousands of refugees were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you receive the reports from the -- these delegations? Did you discuss it? Did you draw any conclusions on the basis of these reports as the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The first one was a delegation of the parliament. The second one was a party delegation where you had talks between HDZ and SDA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were meeting there in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the parliament, did it discuss this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: They did submit a report. Then these conclusions were considered, and we required of the government to do everything that is possible together with the international community in order to scale down and to conclude this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the parliament vote for and earmark special funds in the budget in order to assist Muslims as refugees in Croatia and for Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, be it in clothing, also weapons, for purchasing aid for these Muslims? That I'm asking for the year 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The budget was adopted, and items were also earmarked for humanitarian aid. Regardless, irrespective if the refugees were Muslims, Croatians or Hungarians. No distinction was drawn between the people who were banished, who were refugees. It was a very important item. Because at a certain point we had up to 1 million refugees flowing and coming into the Republic of Croatia. As far as the aid to Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, and weapons, the Republic of Croatia, as you know, had been disarmed by the Yugoslav People's Army in 1990. It collected the weapons of the Territorial Defence. It collected these arms and later it distributed them in the occupied areas of Croatia. It didn't have many possibilities, as an occupied country which is exposed to aggression, to allocate funds for the arming either of Muslims or Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was not a soldier. I -- the weapons came in with volunteers who were living in Croatia and are still living in Croatia, some 500.000 of them. These are 500 Croats who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina and moved to Croatia after the ceasefire. They came as volunteers, went to Bosnia and Herzegovina to defend their towns and their villages, to defend it against occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you personally go to Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Under what conditions and under what circumstances and why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Knowing what is in store for the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and what is being prepared by the greater Serbian aggression in 1992 and after the massacre in Vukovar, other towns in Croatia where even today we are still discovering mass graves. Up till now, 134 mass graves have been discovered, mass graves where corpses of Croats were put in. After the massacre of Muslims in Bijeljina and Eastern Bosnia, we knew of the plan of the so-called "Yugoslav People's Army" and of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbian units. It burnt land which -- and this plan referred to Herzegovina and that the same had to be carried out as in eastern Croatia and some other areas. And as my mother and my brothers lived and still live in Herzegovina, I went, my own free will, to see what is happening, to determine what is happening and to see how to help in order to prevent the worst from happening, namely, occupation, murder, and eviction of Croats from this area of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Only of Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I'm speaking of Croats, because in my town only Croats live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: And otherwise, all of those and Muslims and Croats and others who are of a different ethnicity were taken care of both in Herzegovina as well as in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of the reasons of the conflict of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the HVO in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: I do have some personal knowledge. I believe it is also the truth. Can I -- do you allow me to spend a minute or two? Namely, after the occupation of a part of Croatia, arms, weapons, were withdrawn from Slovenia and from the free part of Croatia towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was done by the JNA, which at the time was totally transformed and became the Serbian army. And after the proclamation at the end of 1991 of the Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then after the eviction and the expelling of the Muslim people from Bijeljina and Foca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if the witness has this knowledge out of his experience at the time he was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because if not, I don't think that this witness should testify on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. We also have the same wondering here. Witness, we want to hear the testimonies of what you have seen and what you have heard during that period. So would you please tell us whether it is your personal experience at the time you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I visited repeatedly Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, and my knowledge is coming from the people who participated in the defence, and it's based on the reports which were coming in daily concerning the events taking place in certain areas. And I intended to give you an assessment, because my opinion concerning -- I intended to give you a political opinion of the conflict between Muslims and Croats in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise. Witness, we are interested whether you participated in negotiations, whether you are -- have observed the conflict. We will skip -- we have some five or six more questions which I would like to clarify, because I believe they concern your personal knowledge. The first question is what do you personally know about the establishment of the HZ HB and reasons behind it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: After the Serbs formed the Krajinas in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, and they were later on incorporated in Republika Srpska in 1991, and after the Muslims formed the Patriotic League as their military component in 1993 and called it the Muslim armed forces, the Croat people could do nothing but to try and organise its forces in its territories because there was no common army. There was the Yugoslav People's Army, which had sided with one people, and the system simply stopped functioning in any respect, from payments, domestic currency, national legal tender, and all the other determinants which enable normal functions of municipalities and citizens in that area. There was no other way without but to form a community, a framework in which they tried to organise life insofar as it was possible under the conditions. When the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, when the Serbian army destroyed Croat villages in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina lived from Ravno on, they did not get support from Sarajevo. Moreover, Alija Izetbegovic said that it was not his war, and in Trebinje, a Muslim representative, Zulfikarpasic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Vucurevic delivered speeches together for joint rallies, and for the camera, Mr. Vucurevic, head of Trebinje, in 1991 said that east Herzegovina will become an integral part of Yugoslavia with the capital in Dubrovnik. Would you believe that? And I wonder what else -- what else could the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina expect and what could they do? So.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me. No, no, no. Finish your sentence. What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: And they created this Croat community of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I've read their statute, their programme of work. It is no special state within a state. It is a temporary, that is what it says a provisional institution pending the end of hostilities and the new order in Bosnia-Herzegovina to organise, to help, to care for life in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And to round off this subject with my final question and then we shall move on to my last couple of questions. Can you agree with the allegation, namely with the following allegation: Namely, the Prosecution here claims that the HZ HB and then HR HB was under the auspices of the Republic of Croatia with a view to joining the Republic of Croatia. What can you say about that? And let me complete this question. It is also alleged ethnically cleansed, meaning non-Croats.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The HZ HB is defined by the statute on the establishment of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Republic of Croatia did not consider that organisation, that institution its ward, because the representatives who represented the Croat community Herceg-Bosna did not come from one political party but, rather, from all the political parties of the Croat people founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is an institution which represented the entire Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They took their decisions autonomously, independently, not having to do anything with Republic of Croatia, except that I was present as a guest at some of the conventions of the HZ HB, but it represented all the representatives elected to the parliament, to the municipal boards elected by the people, and we were there as guests without participating in their deliberations, without decision making powers, without any persuasion, I repeat merely as guests from the Republic of Croatia. And that that ethnically cleansed territory would then be annexed to Croatia? Well, to ethnically cleanse, this is my opinion. I take it that is Muslims who are meant, that is cleansing Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Well, Muslims and Croats are -- worked together in 1993 in the Croat Defence Council. They waged war against one aggressor, and when they wouldn't be arming their future adversaries if they were planning to cleanse them from the territory some time. Throughout that time in Mostar, on the west bank, there were ten thousand Muslims living. And as far as I know, only about 100 or so Croats remained on the east bank. There was no ethnic cleansing, nor was that the policy of either the HZ HB and let alone the policy of the Croatian state and the Croatian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you because you have been a member of the Croatian diet from the very first day and I'm telling you what the Prosecution is alleging in this case. Of course they have to prove it yet. But you as a representative, as a MP, do you think that anyone could take such a decision apart from the Croatian diet, I mean about the annexation or anything else? Let me just complete this and round this off. So did the Croatian national diet ever deliver it or can anyone apart from the Croatian national diet take a decision on such annexations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The Croatian national diet never discussed it. No political party in Croatian has something like that in its programme, be it left or right or centrist party. These are insinuations. There were no public, private, secret meetings rarely that would promote such an aspiration to annex an adjacent part of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia, even Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. though the latest report that I've read, Mr. Jacques Klein in Sarajevo said recently that Alija Izetbegovic had been offering to President Tudjman a part of Bosnia, but President Tudjman, of course, refused it as unfair, as unfeasible, as unacceptable because it would do away with his well-known position on the recognition of former republics based on their recognised borders and Croatian won recognition for that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. Let us move on to our last topic, and may I ask Mrs. -- The registrar, that is to give to the usher D1/328 and D1/329. They've both been translated into English. That is what I promised Judge Clark before this witness. We have translated all the laws on archives on the confidentiality and all the other laws. There are three or four of them, and especially those that you will see. Now they have to do with the archives, archives left behind late President Franjo Tudjman. Mr. Kovac, are these the laws which were passed by the Croatian national diet?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Only briefly, basically because the document speaks for itself, which are the laws? Just a sentence or two.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The law on the archives -- just let me see. On the protection of the confidentiality of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Since you were one of those who passed this law, do you know how the archives, how the documents are kept in view of the national security in the Croatian state, for how long they are to be kept under seal and under what conditions they may be disclosed to third persons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Any use and storing of archival material or documents of national interest, of state interest, all such documents are kept pursuant to articles of this law on the archives passed by the Croatian diet in 1996. And before that, the laws which were taken over from the former state were in force to avoid a legal rancor. It is clearly specified how documents are stored in the state archive of the Republic of Croatia, who may have access to it, who may use it and how, and in particular, the archives, as specified in Article 20 of the law on archival documents in archives, which specifies that the archives containing data relative to the defence and international relations matters of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Just do go on but slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: And in particular Article 20, which -- the latter part of which I will quote, which now specifies which of the materials, which are the documents of national or state interest and how they are disposed of and how they are stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You don't have to do that because everybody has this law before him. It's been translated and the document speaks for itself. So let us not waste time. I merely wanted to ask you briefly: Are you familiar with this document? Because after all, you're a member of the legislature. For how many years are they placed under seal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Thirty years. Nobody can take out or use such documents. And the law also specifies how -- prescribes the procedure in which one may use it and how, but only subject to the approval of the government and the diet or, rather, the board for national security of the Croatian national diet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You see there are all sorts of documents here which are claimed to have come from the Zagreb archives, but we'll come to another topic. And it also seethes with what was termed here presidential transcripts, that is allegedly transcript that were done in the president's office. But that is another subject. Does the official confidentiality law or archives specify how such a document may get to this Court? Not the Court, the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, the law prescribes how these documents can be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, does the president of the state, if he does not act in accordance with this law, violate this law and, therefore, may be called to account? I mean, if the president of the State of Croatia, is this law binding on him as on everybody else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm just reading this question. Does the official confidentiality law specify how this document gets to this Court and the answer is yes, but can we be more specific as to which law says so or which article? I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, you might rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We are now talking about two laws, the archives law and the official -- and confidentiality law. And my question is whether the president of the state violates the same law if he does not behave in accordance with those laws.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the citizens of every state, and the same goes for the president, must abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, let us look at D1/301, 302, 303, and 323. And as we are waiting for them, let me ask you, did the diet discuss or did they talk about the records kept in the office of the -- of the president of the republic, which are known here as presidential transcripts? Did they discuss it and what decisions were taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The diet -- the diet did discuss it. And on the basis of that, the law was amended, the archives law and confidentiality law was amended, and the diet empowered the government of the Republic of Croatia to adopt a special decree to regulate the use of the documents emanating from President Tudjman's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the decision taken by the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: May I read the decision of the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, because I'm mixed up with all the different exhibit numbers. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, could you please mention when documents bear a number so that we can follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is 302, because the numbering was changed at about five to eleven in consultation with Madam Registrar. I believe this is Exhibit 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was the old number? Because that doesn't help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 321, D1/321 it says on the document. And right after that is document 322 to which I will come next, and then 323. These are the three laws that we shall be talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, let's look at the first document which is marked, as you can see, 321. This is the old number. Are you familiar with this decision? What year does it date to, and what did it set out to regulate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Three?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: 321 it says down at the bottom. It is decree on the way and procedure to be required.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the decision of the government of the Republic of Croatia. It was taken on the 16th of December, 1999. And I was a Minister in that cabinet, and I know why such a decision was taken on the way and procedure to be applied to the selection and setting aside of recordings or documents produced under the activity of Dr. Franjo Tudjman. Following the president's death in 1999, the Croatian media began to carry documents from the president's office which were, incidentally, not authentic and those which were -- and those who were mentioned in those transcripts filed suits against those who disclosed those documents to the public without due authority. The government of the Republic of Croatia, therefore, passed this decision to regulate and prescribe in which way we'll file and store the documents and who may have access to these archives. The president's office was made responsible for the implementation of this decision. You have it before you, so I will not quote from it. After the elections on the 3rd of January, 2000, after the presidential elections in the beginning of 2000, media continued to carry documents from the president's office, violating the confidentiality law and the archives law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which was the main problem? You said something about "in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beginning." Did the government take this decision because the authenticity had not been established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: One of the reasons was the non-authenticity of the documents as publicly shown in the statements and in court of those who figured in those so-called transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the diet's board -- about the parliamentary boards discuss this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Correct. The national security board and the other boards concerned discussed the problem which caused the indignation of the Croatian public. And as to the diet's proposal, the government, the newly elected government, on the 11th of January, 2001, adopted the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are we talking now about document 323?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the decision of that government, the current government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This government, on the 11th of January, after the parliamentary discussion and after its discussion by the boards, the government of the Republic of Croatia was made responsible for taking a decision which we have before us on the taking over and use of the documentation produced under the activity of Dr. Franjo Tudjman in his capacity as president of Croatia, and this was signed by Mr. Goran Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are these documents being placed unseal and does this document question the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Croatia is not called upon to establish the authenticity of the documents under this decision, as it transpires clearly from item 2 of this decision. And for how many years are these documents, alleged presidential transcripts, placed unseal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: These -- this is regulated by the archives and confidentiality laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. I see. Your Honours, is this time for a break? And we have a judge of the supreme court from my state who is now listening, so I'm struck by stage fright. But I have two questions, I believe, and then I'll be finishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you only have two questions, why not continue to finish these two questions? After that, we will have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. So, Mr. Kovac, before I finish, I have two short questions. One of the documents which we did not address so far, and it's old number 320. Will you tell Their Honours, 320, old number, will you explain to the Chamber, what does this declaration mean? Was it adopted by the diet, why, and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: After long deliberations in the Croatian public, media, and beyond, which never stopped asking whether the patriotic war in the Republic of Croatia was a liberation war, was it a war of aggression, whether the Republic of Croatia in the 1990s had launched an aggression against other state, whether it set out to occupy another state, and so two years ago the Croatian national diet, in the year 2000 included in its agenda the problems and the definition of truth about the Croatian policy in the 1990s and the character of the war, the nature of war in Croatia and the attitude of Croatia towards other republics. Unanimously, all the parliamentary parties in the Croatian diet adopted this declaration by consensus, which is of great importance for this Court, because it defines the Republic of Croatia, its attitude towards primarily Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I hear that even here in this Tribunal, in the indictments, gentlemen who are sitting here and others are being told that Croatia had committed an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it wanted to annex parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia. So the diet unanimously voted for this declaration which says that the Republic of Croatia, which the just defensive and liberation war rather than aggressive war, a war of conquest against anyone in which it defended its territory against the -- again the Serbian aggression within its internationally recognised borders. I repeat, by consensus and unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we just have the date of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovac, who would have to -- and what would be the procedure if I, as counsel for Defence, if I asked to see the transcripts from the president's office, which by this government's decision of 1999 and then repeated in 2001 and the laws, what would be the procedure to follow? Could I gain access to them, and what would I have to do in order to gain access to them? And I suppose the same procedure would applied to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: You could gain access to them if you follow the procedure based on law and decisions of the government of the Republic of Croatia in 1999 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Prosecutor of this Tribunal requested the permission of the Croatian national diet concerning the transcripts from the president's office and whether he got such a permission from the either the government or the Croatian national diet? Because I put it to you that here presidential transcripts are being used and claims are made that they're authentic. They are here. Are you aware of that at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC
utterances.text: If that is true, if it is true that there are transcript here in this Court, then I can claim under full responsibility that they are not -- that they have not got here in a lawful manner because the diet or the parliamentary board responsible for security never discussed nor permitted any use of these documents or these archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are we therefore talking about illegal documents?
